extracted.intended_audience: college students and other academic writers deciding whether to use first-person or personal experience
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when to use first-person pronouns and personal experience in academic writing, with field-specific recommendations, examples, alternatives, and stylistic cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide according to purpose, audience, and disciplinary conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because college writing situations vary widely in stylistic conventions, tone, audience, and purpose, decide whether to use first person or personal experience by deciphering the conventions of your writing context and considering your purpose and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout's central rule: choose what suits your purpose as a scholar; instructors may differ so ask them if unsure. Flexibility is important; breaking old rules is sometimes necessary when it improves clarity or effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective uses of first person ('I','we')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use first-person pronouns when they strengthen your writing by emphasizing agency, improving clarity, or positioning the writer in relation to other scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits enumerated: Assertiveness (emphasize who is doing what), Clarity (avoids awkward, vague constructions), Positioning (explain how your research builds on or departs from others and claim authority). Example: 'In our study... we explored...' is clearer than convoluted passive phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid first person when describing objective or reproducible phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: When your purpose is to describe an objective phenomenon independent of your subjective perspective, use impersonal constructions instead of grounding the statement in 'I'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns and examples: avoid 'As I observed the communication styles...' and prefer 'A study of the communication styles... revealed...'; avoid personal framing when you want to create the impression of an observed, reproducible phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't let 'I think/I feel/I believe' replace argumentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid phrases such as 'I think,' 'I feel,' or 'I believe' as mere hedges or substitutes for real evidence or reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers assume the paper expresses the writer's views; instead of prefacing opinions with 'I think,' state the claim and support it with evidence. Example: replace 'I think Aristotle's arguments are logical...' with 'Aristotle's ethical arguments are logical...' and then provide reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field guideline — Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific writing has historically avoided first person to preserve an impression of objectivity, but conventions are changing in some contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally avoid 'I' in lab reports or when describing observations that must be reproducible; however, first person may be acceptable when describing a project you are conducting or positioning it within research. Always check with the course instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field guideline — Social Sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Social sciences sometimes avoid 'I' for objectivity, but first person is becoming more accepted, especially when describing your project or perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person selectively when situating your research or methodology; consider disciplinary norms and instructor preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field guideline — Humanities
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers in the humanities often value assertiveness and agency, so first person is often—but not always—appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanities readers expect fully argued and supported assertions; personal belief alone is not sufficient. If you use first person, make sure to defend and illustrate your assertions with evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other situations: speeches and resumes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different writing situations have different norms: public-facing or performative genres often favor personal pronouns, while formal documents may avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches: use first and even second person ('you') to create connection and sincerity. Resumes: avoid the first person; write experience and accomplishments without personal pronouns (e.g., 'Volunteered as a peer counselor').

rubrics_metrics.name: Second person ('you') is usually inappropriate in academic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'you' can sound overly conversational or presumptive in most academic contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for an academic tone, prefer alternatives such as 'one,' 'the reader,' or 'people.' Only use 'you' when a conversational tone or direct address suits the purpose (e.g., this handout, letters, or speeches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal experience: use depends on context and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether personal experience belongs in academic writing depends on the assignment's goals; it may distract from objectivity in some fields but serve as legitimate evidence in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert personal experience in objective/data-driven papers (e.g., many science papers) unless you are explicitly situating yourself as researcher. Personal experience can be used to present individual responses to art, illustrate how theory applies to life, or demonstrate an abstract principle. Keep such accounts brief and clearly tied to the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal experience should serve the argument and be kept brief
rubrics_metrics.description: If you include a real or hypothetical story, it must support your analytical or argumentative goals rather than become the focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: keep anecdotes short, explicitly connect them to your point, and avoid letting them take over the paper. Use personal experience sparingly to add concreteness or vitality when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective ways to incorporate personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Use anecdotes, references to your own experience to explain interest or authority, or follow assignment prompts that request personal material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of legitimate uses: brief illustrative anecdotes in philosophy to show abstract ideas, references that explain why you are interested in a topic, and application essays that explicitly request personal history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy-specific guidance on personal examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical writing can legitimately use real or hypothetical scenarios to illustrate abstract arguments, including invented or recounted situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using such scenarios, always explain to the reader how the experience or example relates to and supports your argument. See additional writing-in-philosophy resources for more guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion-specific guidance on personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Although religion topics may seem to invite personal testimony, many religion courses emphasize cultural, historical, or textual approaches that require objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let personal beliefs replace scholarly analysis; personal experiences may be appropriate in less formal assignments like response papers—ask your instructor when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature/film/music/fine arts guidance on personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal observations can sometimes be appropriate in analyses of creative works if they are relevant and not tangential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal annoyance about a roommate is not relevant to analyzing Citizen Kane; but relevant personal observations can inform analysis (e.g., how audiences experience a film). Response papers and reception-oriented scholarship may welcome such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's Studies guidance on personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: In Women's Studies, personal experience is often useful as evidence because the field values accounts of how individuals experience gender roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments may require journals or reflective writing that apply theory to personal experience; use such directives as opportunities to incorporate personal material as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: History guidance on personal experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal experience is generally less appropriate when analyzing historical periods, though historical scholarship may explore the personal histories of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are more likely to discuss other people's experiences as illustrations of historical context than to use your own experience as evidence for general historical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sciences guidance on personal experience (reiteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific contexts, personal experience is usually out of place; in social sciences, case studies of others' experiences are important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lab reports should describe observations in reproducible terms rather than personal narrative. In social science case studies, descriptions of subjects' experiences are often essential and appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternatives to first person when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If first person is not appropriate, use impersonal constructions, passive voice, or noun phrases to express the same idea without 'I' or 'we.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: change 'As I was reading this study... I noticed...' to 'This study... reveals...' or 'A study of... revealed...' These alternatives can create a more academic tone and stronger, clearer statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When in doubt, ask the instructor
rubrics_metrics.description: Because disciplinary and instructor expectations vary, consult the instructor to determine whether first person or personal experience is appropriate for a specific assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The handout repeatedly advises checking with the course instructor when uncertain about style conventions.
